• Name: Signal crayfish
  • Scientific name: Pacifastacus leniusculus
  • Other names: the California crayfish
  • Minimum tank size: about 60 litres
  • Breeding: easy
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: aggressive
  • Colour: dark brown

Important: Pacifastacus leniusculus (the Signal crayfish) is one of the most widespread and most successful invasive crayfish species in Europe. Even if it is not banned in your state or country, NEVER release the Signal crayfish into the wild! Pacifastacus leniusculus carries crayfish plague (Aphanomyces astaci), to which it is resistant but which is lethal to most other crayfish species. In addition, it can alter ecosystems, causing the loss of native species, harming fisheries, and having major economic consequences.

Are Signal crayfish plant safe? No, they are not. Signal crayfish will eat, cut, and shred almost any plant they can get.

It is not recommended to keep them in planted tanks. The only viable options for this species are:

  • plastic plants,
  • floating plants,
  • some cheap plants that you are ready to lose.

Pacifastacus leniusculus is endemic to northwestern America and southwestern Canada. Nowadays, these crayfish can be found in over 20 countries in Europe (Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Russian Federation, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom), Asia and even South Africa.

Interesting fact: Signal crayfish were widely introduced into many parts of Europe and Asia in the mid- to late 1900s to compensate for the loss of native European and Asian species caused by the crayfish plague. The sad thing though is that that plague started from the previous introduction of this species. Unfortunately, the mistake was discovered when it was already too late.

The Signal crayfish inhabit freshwater bodies such as ponds, lakes, streams, rivers, and even low-salinity waters.

This species does not have a preference and can be found in rocky, muddy, and vegetated areas.

Crayfish need a lot of space to move in the tank. A 60-litre tank is the recommended minimum for one adult Signal crayfish. Juveniles can be kept in smaller tanks but will quickly outgrow them.

Main reasons to have a larger tank:

  • The bigger the tank, the easier it is to set up diverse areas for them to dwell and hide.
  • Crayfish produce a lot of waste, so it can be easier to keep water parameters stable.

Important: Signal crayfish are great escape artists and will climb air hoses and silicone sealant, so you should place a fitted lid on the tank. When keeping any type of crayfish, make sure the water line in your aquarium is not too high.

If you are a first-time crayfish owner, it is important to cycle your tank before bringing any crayfish home. Once the tank is cycled, check the water quality using a test kit.

Temperature: Signal crayfish do not like too warm temperatures. According to the experiments, the ultimate upper lethal temperature for this species was 31.1°C.

Note: After 70 days at 25°C, crayfish became sluggish. Survival dropped drastically above 26°C and some crayfish started dying from an abnormal molt.

Thus, their preferred water temperature is 10–21°C. This range is considered optimal for the Signal crayfish.

pH: Signal crayfish require water with a pH greater than 7.0. Ideally, pH should be in the range of 7.0–8.5.

Note: Low pH impedes the crayfish's calcium absorption and thus weakens their carapaces, which increases mortality.

Hardness: They will appreciate an optimal KH of 3–20 and a GH between 3 and 25.

Salinity: Signal crayfish are hardy enough to tolerate salinity for some time. Experiments showed that they survive over 9 weeks at salinities up to 28 PSU. However, egg-bearing females have not been seen at salinities above 7 PSU.

Substrate: As long as there are many hiding places, there is no need for a deep substrate. However, if you decide to have one, a steeply sloping bed suitable for burrowing is the best choice. Avoid completely flat and soft bottoms. In their natural habitat, the percentage of the bed covered with cobbles and small stones typically varies between 7% and 100%.

Lighting: No special requirements. Signal crayfish are nocturnal. If you have plants, lighting should be adapted to their needs.

Filtration: Sponge filters in a tank with Signal crayfish are a very bad idea, as these crayfish will chip, chew and break apart the sponge. Hang-on-back or canister filters are a better choice.

Decorations: Shelter is an important and limited resource for crayfish. Signal crayfish often hide in shelters under driftwood, between rocks, and in burrows. Thus artificial shelters are essential and should be abundant. Providing shelter during the mating season is important as it offers protection during vulnerable periods such as molting, protects the brood stock against predation, and minimizes aggressive interactions. Stacks of PVC pipes, mesh bundles, driftwood, etc. provide enough shelter, especially in the grow-out phase.

Signal crayfish are benthic omnivorous and detritivorous feeders.

It means that they can feed on a variety of items. According to the study, a total of 22 food groups were categorized from their gut contents, including fish eggs and larvae, insects, macroinvertebrates (snails, worms, other crayfish, etc.), small invertebrates (tadpoles, etc.), algae, macrophytes, dead leaves, plants, etc.

Direct predation of fish, as well as cannibalism, occurred. However, fish are mostly preyed upon by adult Signal crayfish. Cannibalism increased mainly with crayfish size.

Note: There is some conflicting information regarding juvenile crayfish. In most crayfish species, juveniles are primarily carnivorous to gain a clear growth advantage. However, there are also reports that, in Signal crayfish, juveniles consumed food types that were just the opposite of those purported to be of most nutritional value to them (such as detrital matter, needles, leaves, etc.).

Detritus and green algae (Cladophora) are ingested most frequently by crayfish of all sizes throughout the year.

Signal crayfish mainly feed at night. The estimated daily ration ranged from 0.22 to 6.02% of wet body weight.

In captivity, for the best growth, the diet should consist of about 80% vegetation and 20% protein-based food.

If kept as pets in aquariums, suggested foods include:

  • leaves,
  • plants,
  • vegetables,
  • crushed snails,
  • earthworms,
  • brine shrimp,
  • dead fish or shrimp,
  • Artemia sp.,
  • shrimp pellets,
  • shrimp granules,
  • shrimp food (crustacean food such as Hikari Shrimp Cuisine),
  • frozen bloodworms, etc.

Features:

  • Food preference: a mix of meat and vegetation.
  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week for adults. Daily for juveniles.

Rules of diet in captivity:

  • Leave their food for 24 hours before removing it. To prevent water contamination, remove leftover food by siphoning before adding fresh food. Leaves can be left for several days in the tank.
  • Leave old exoskeletons. Do not remove molted exoskeletons. They will eat them later.
  • Check their hiding places. Signal crayfish often drag and store food in their hiding spots for later consumption. Check them from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination.
  • Crayfish need diversity in food. Do not give them the same food all the time. Change their diet periodically.

Crayfish are fully aquatic animals. They need a permanent water body to survive since they live in open water.

Signal crayfish are highly nocturnal, according to the study, with less than 6% of movements recorded during daylight hours. Generally, they emerge from their hiding places to forage after dark and are capable of substantial active movements.

These crayfish are classified as secondary burrowers. It means that they do not rely on burrows and do not spend all of their time there. However, if the environment (substrate) allows, they may dig burrows.

Signal crayfish dig very simple, straight burrows with somewhat angular chambers and a single opening below the water surface. In most cases, their depth ranges from 15 to 65 cm.

Interesting facts:

  • Unlike the majority of smaller crayfish, large males (over 10 cm) rarely make burrows even when there are no natural shelters. This is probably because large males have bigger and more powerful claws than females and/or juveniles and do not seem to shelter from potential predators that often.
  • Juveniles can make a burrow within an hour, whereas adults may often spend several hours or even days completing the excavation.
  • When they return to the burrows, they check them for intruders before they enter (tail first).

Signal crayfish are territorial and need a lot of space to reduce their naturally aggressive temperament. However, their aggression can decline as both shelter and food become more available.

Features:

  • Social: no
  • Active: no
  • Peaceful: no
  • Territorial: yes
  • Burrowers: yes

Tankmates: Pacifastacus leniusculus is an aggressive and territorial species, so it is right to say Signal crayfish have no suitable tankmates.

These crayfish are hostile to fish, other crayfish species, crabs, dwarf frogs, and especially freshwater snails. Signal crayfish are voracious consumers of freshwater gastropods.

Signal crayfish have been observed going after fish nests at night and preying on fish eggs. In the long run, small community fish and shrimp have no chance against their claws.

At the same time, larger and/or aggressive fish will hunt Signal crayfish.

Overall, it can be quite complicated to keep other animals with Signal crayfish. The ideal setup is a species-only tank with many hiding places to reduce aggressive behaviour.

Pacifastacus leniusculus exhibits obvious sexual dimorphism.

  • Females have a greater total length and a wider abdomen, while males have a higher weight and larger claws than females.
  • Male crayfish lack hooks on the 3rd segment of the walking legs, while females lack the seminal receptacle, which is located between the 4th and 5th pairs of walking legs.

Maturity: Females reach sexual maturity in the 3rd year and males in the 2nd year, at a carapace length of about 36–38 mm or about 8 cm total length.

Note: The smallest berried female recorded had a carapace length of 36.3 mm, corresponding to an age of 2+.

Signal crayfish spawn within one week, usually 2–3 days, after mating.

Note: Only about 90% of females are ready to reproduce annually.

Eggs: There is a positive correlation between female size and the number of eggs, as larger females produce more eggs. According to multiple studies, females can usually have between 130 and 724 eggs per brood. Large females can often carry more than 500 eggs. Eggs are attached to the female throughout the whole embryonic development. Egg diameter and egg weight are 2.40–2.88 mm and 0.007–0.012 g respectively.

In Pacifastacus leniusculus, ovaries mature between July and January; oviposition occurs between October and February; young hatch from May to July. Because of the low temperature in their natural environment, it takes several months for the eggs to hatch.

Note: Experiments showed that females held at an average of 6.8°C failed to hatch eggs.

Hatching: The mean size of newly hatched juveniles is 9.7 mm. After hatching, they remain with their mother for several weeks, then leave as completely independent miniature adults. Generally, brooding females do not cannibalise eggs and young.

With average lengths between 7–10 cm, Signal crayfish are relatively large crayfish. The maximum size collected was about 18 cm.

This species has massive claws that affect their weight. For example, a 7–8 cm male and female generally weigh 158 g and 115 g respectively.

Signal crayfish are easily identified by the white colour on the underside of their large and robust claws. The overall colour is dark brown.

Lifespan: according to the study, Signal crayfish are long-lived. Based on a neuronal age pigment, the average estimated longevity is between 6 and 16 years, with some individuals able to live up to 20 years.

Growth: according to the study, these crayfish grow fast, reaching 10 cm total length after only 3 years. Such individuals molt only once a year, while younger ones molt more often, for example:

  • 2 times (crayfish smaller than 7–8 cm)
  • 3 times (crayfish smaller than 5 cm)

After hatching, the juveniles molt for the first time after 2 weeks. After 3 months, they grow to 26.5 mm.

Crayfish are highly vulnerable to predation and adverse environmental factors during molting.

Interesting fact: males grow faster than females, with a larger increment per molt and more frequent molts.

In conclusion: the Signal crayfish is a very easy animal to care for in a home aquarium, even for beginners. Nonetheless, be very careful and never release them into the wild.

Pacifastacus leniusculus is very tolerant of environmental extremes, such as temperature and various pollutants. Its aggressive nature, combined with its prolific breeding habits, allows it to out-compete most other crayfish species.
